title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
Working with measurements

Chemometrics is the application of mathematics and statistics to chemical measurements
In practice, this mostly means creating algorithms to:

process and interpret single measurements
compare and contrast multiple measurements
compile multiple measurements as databases (libraries)
search libraries
classify measurements

title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
Searching measurement libraries

Let \(\mathbf{X}=\{X_1, X_2,...,X_n\}\) be a library of measurements 
Let \(U\) be the measurement of an unknown
Let \(d_i = f(U,X_i)\) be the numerical distance between the unknown measurement and library measurement \(i\)
In library searching, we compute \(\mathbf{d} = (d_1, d_2, ..., d_n)\)

title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
Searching measurement libraries

We then generate a Hit List of the top \(k\) most similar measurements from the library \(\mathbf{H}=\text{top}_k(\text{sort}(\mathbf{X},\text{by } \mathbf{d}))\) 
We inspect \(\mathbf{H}\) and try to determine which (if any) of the measurements in \(\mathbf{H}\):

are a potential identity for \(U\), or
have information that can help us interpret \(U\)

title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
Searching measurement libraries

Start by clearing work space, loading custom functions, and loading a pre-compiled library (note to arun, explain the library structure to students)



## Step 0. Clear up the work space, load custom functions, load the reference mass spectral library
rm(list=ls()) # clears up the work space
source("CustomFunctions/LibrarySearchFunctions.R") # loads all the functions in the file
Library = readRDS("asm_ReferenceMSLibrary_SWDRUG314.RDS") # loads the reference library

title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
Searching measurement libraries

Load up an unknown, define the metric used to compare the unknown to the library spectra, and define the number of results that will be returned as a hit list



Unknown = read.table("Unknowns/U1.txt")  # reads in the unknown mass spectrum
Metric = "Euclidean"                     # this can take one of two values "Euclidean" or "CosineSim"
nHits = 10                               # this is the number of most similar library entries we want returned

Results = LibrarySearch(Unknown,Library,Metric,nHits) # This returns the library search HitList and RunTime. 

View(Results$HitList)
cat(Results$RunTime)

title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
More on library searches

Library searches are \(O(n)\) time-complex algorithms, this means they scale linearly with the size of the problem

E.g., if it takes 10 seconds to search a library with 10 entries, it will take 3600 seconds to search library with 3600 entries 

Most of the entries in your library won’t be relevant, especially if you are using a big commercial library
Using a clever “pre-search” (i.e., a filter to make your library smaller) will help speed up your library search algorithm


Time permits, show the students NIST MS Search via remote access

title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
Distance Matrices and Multidimensional scaling

In a library search, we compare one unknown to a library of \(n\) entries; this tells us how similar the unknown is to each element of the library

It does not tell us how similar the library entries are too each other

Given a set of measurement (e.g., a library or otherwise), it can be informative to compute an \(n\times n\) distance matrix \(\mathbf{D}\) from \(\mathbf{X}\) such that  \(D_{i,j} = d(X_i,X_j)\)
This matrix is the input to several useful algorithms

title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
A first distance matrix


U = seq(1,30)
D = array(0,dim=c(length(U),length(U)))

for(i in 1:length(U)){
  indices_i = which(Library$SpectralData$SpecID==U[i])
  spec_mz_i = Library$SpectralData$mz[indices_i]
  spec_int = Library$SpectralData$int[indices_i]
  spec_int_i = spec_int/max(spec_int)
  
  for(j in 1:length(U)){
    
    indices_j = which(Library$SpectralData$SpecID==U[j])
    spec_mz_j = Library$SpectralData$mz[indices_j]
    spec_int = Library$SpectralData$int[indices_j]
    spec_int_j = spec_int/max(spec_int)

    maxmz = max(spec_mz_i,spec_mz_j)
    A = spec2vec(spec_mz_i,spec_int_i,maxmz)
    B = spec2vec(spec_mz_j,spec_int_j,maxmz)
    
    D[i,j] = 1-cosineSim(A,B)
  }

}

title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
A dendrogram (hierarchical clustering)

a fun algorithm for grouping together measurements based on minimal distance is called agglomerative hierarchical clustering (AHC)

every measurement starts as its own cluster
the two closest clusters are combined, then the next two, then the next two… until there is one big agglomerate cluster
analyst needs to define “closest” in the clustering space




D = as.dist(D)
ClusterResults = hclust(D,method="complete")
plot(ClusterResults)

title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
Multidimensional Scaling

multidimensional scaling is an algorithm that identifies a \(k\)-dimensional configuration that maintains the gives the same (or near same) distance matrix as the original distance matrix; \(k\) is some selected dimensionality of the output configuration



mds = cmdscale(D,k=2)
rownames(mds) = U
plot(mds,pch=19,cex=0)
text(mds[,1],mds[,2],U)

title: Projection and dimensionality reduction
text:
Principal Component Analysis

principal component analysis (PCA) is an incredibly popular method for projecting higher dimensional data into a lower dimensional space



U = seq(1,30)
data = array(0,dim=c(length(U),1000))
for(i in 1:length(U)){
  indices = which(Library$SpectralData$SpecID==i)
  mz = Library$SpectralData$mz[indices]
  int = Library$SpectralData$int[indices]
  data[i,] = spec2vec(mz,int,1000)
}

zeros = which(colSums(data)==0)
data = data[,-zeros]
pca_results = prcomp(data)
scores = pca_results$x[,1:2,drop=FALSE]
plot(scores,cex=0)
text(scores[,1],scores[,2],U)

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
From interpreting to comparing

To this point, we’ve worked with individual mass spectra (as a representative measurement)

we looked at loading the measurement
plotting it
processing it (e.g., removing peaks)
interpreting it (e.g., identifying the base peak, identifying significant peaks)

In addition to looking at individual measurements, we often want to compare measurements

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
Comparing two mass spectra

Load and plot two mass spectra



SpecA = read.table("U1.txt")
mzA = SpecA[,1]
intA = SpecA[,2]/max(SpecA[,2])

SpecB = read.table("U2.txt")
mzB = SpecB[,1]
intB = SpecB[,2]/max(SpecB[,2])


plot(mzA,
     intA,
     type="h",
     xlab="mass-to-charge ratio",
     ylab="relative intensity") 

plot(mzB,
     intB,
     type="h",
     xlab="mass-to-charge ratio",
     ylab="relative intensity")

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
Comparing two mass spectra

In MS, it is common to create head-to-tail plots to compare and contrast mass spectra



minx = min(mzA,mzB)
maxx = max(mzA,mzB)

plot(mzA,
     intA,
     type="h",
     xlab="mass-to-charge ratio",
     ylab="relative intensity",
     xlim=c(minx,maxx),
     ylim=c(-1,1),
     col="purple") 

matplot(mzB,
        -intB,
        type="h",
        col="blue",
        add=TRUE)

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
Comparing two mass spectra

When we compare and contrast data, we are really looking for similarities and differences

number of common peaks?
number of common major peaks?
fraction of common major peaks compared to all peaks?
fraction of total relative intensity accounted for by common peaks?

IMPORTANT: We need to explicitly define metrics of similarity (or differences) to support rigorous comparison and transparent communications

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
On vectors

Vectors are mathematical objects that can be thought of as points in higher dimensional space

E.g., used in chemistry and physics to describe objects with multiple properties (e.g., magnitude and direction)

From geometry, we have some standard methods for comparing vectors 
Consider the 2D vectors (1,5) and (7,3)

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text: Comparing vectors

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
Comparing vectors

Distance

How far are the vectors in n-dimensional space
Euclidean Distance:  \(d(x,y) = \sqrt{\sum_i^n(x_i-y_i)^2}\)

Similarity

A function of the angle between the vectors in n-dimensional space
Cosine Similarity:  \(s(x,y) = \frac{\sum_i^n x_iy_i}{\sqrt{\sum_i^n x_i^2}\sqrt{\sum_i^n y_i^2}}\)

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
Comparing vectors

A = c(1,5)
B = c(7,3)

ED = sqrt(sum((A-B)^2))
CS = sum(A*B)/(sqrt(sum(A*A))*sqrt(sum(B*B)))
cat(paste0("The euclidean distance between vectors A and B is ",round(ED,3),"\n"))
cat(paste0("The cosine similarity between vectors A and B is ",round(CS,3),"\n"))


A = c(1,5,5,7,6,8)
B = c(7,3,2,8,9,1)

ED = sqrt(sum((A-B)^2))
CS = sum(A*B)/(sqrt(sum(A*A))*sqrt(sum(B*B)))
cat(paste0("The euclidean distance between vectors A and B is ",round(ED,3),"\n"))
cat(paste0("The cosine similarity between vectors A and B is ",round(CS,3),"\n"))


A = c(1,5,0,0)
B = c(7,3,0,0)

ED = sqrt(sum((A-B)^2))
CS = sum(A*B)/(sqrt(sum(A*A))*sqrt(sum(B*B)))
cat(paste0("The euclidean distance between vectors A and B is ",round(ED,3),"\n"))
cat(paste0("The cosine similarity between vectors A and B is ",round(CS,3),"\n"))

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
From mass spectra to vectors

If we can represent our mass spectral measurements as comparable vectors, we can use the idea of distances and similarities as an objective way to compare mass spectra

a standard approach with low-resolution (integer resolution) mass spectra is to create vectors that are the length of the highest m/z value and populate the vector such that the value at each index of the vector is the intensity from the corresponding m/z in the spectrum

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
From mass spectra to vectors

SpecA = read.table("U1.txt")
mzA = SpecA[,1]
intA = SpecA[,2]/max(SpecA[,2])

A = numeric(max(mzA)) # create a numeric vector the length of the highest mass to charge ratio in A filled with zeros
A[129:136]

[1] 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0

for(i in 1:length(mzA)){
  A[mzA[i]] = intA[i]
}
A[129:136]

[1] 0.058058058 0.010010010 0.003003003 0.015015015 0.029029029 0.064064064
[7] 0.007007007 0.001001001

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
From mass spectra to vectors

IMPORTANT: When comparing two vectors, they must be of the same dimension

If two mass spectra have different highest mass-to-charge ratios; we make sure the vectors created by these mass spectra take the length of the higher of the two mass-to-charge ratios

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
From mass spectra to vectors

SpecA = read.table("U1.txt")
mzA = SpecA[,1]
intA = SpecA[,2]/max(SpecA[,2])

SpecB = read.table("U2.txt")
mzB = SpecB[,1]
intB = SpecB[,2]/max(SpecB[,2])

maxMz = max(c(mzA,mzB))
A = numeric(maxMz)
B = numeric(maxMz)

for(i in 1:length(mzA)){
  A[mzA[i]] = intA[i]
}

for(i in 1:length(mzB)){
  B[mzB[i]] = intB[i]
}

ED = sqrt(sum((A-B)^2))
CS = sum(A*B)/(sqrt(sum(A*A))*sqrt(sum(B*B)))
cat(paste0("The euclidean distance between vectors A and B is ",round(ED,3),"\n"))

The euclidean distance between vectors A and B is 1.627

cat(paste0("The cosine similarity between vectors A and B is ",round(CS,3),"\n"))

The cosine similarity between vectors A and B is 0.06

title: Similarities and differences (distances)
text:
From mass spectra to vectors

We can be selective (and more efficient) when constructing a vector embedding of a mass spectrum

Domain-segmented similarity score: This is a new article I wrote where we are trying to use contextual knowledge when comparing high resolution mass spectra

We can also experiment with other measures of similarity and distances

Pattern similarity measures: This is an old article I wrote where we compare several standard measures of similarity used in pattern recognition to more “customized” measures found in the mass spectrometry literature

title: What is a measurement?
text:
What is a sample?


 A sample is a physical material we are trying to identify (or classify or safely dispose of or otherwise deal with)

Usually a subset of a larger population
Insights from the sample may allow us to infer something about the population

title: What is a measurement?
text:
What is a structure?


 A structure is a human-defined representation of the relationship between the atoms that constitute a compound

Names [common vs IUPAC]
Encodings [SMILES vs InChI vs InChIKey]

Diagrams [Line drawings]

How materials are described; How materials are scheduled

title: What is a measurement?
text:
What is a measurement?

A measurement is a quantity that characterizes some physical or phenomenological property of a sample 
In analytical (forensic) chemistry, a measurement is a feature that can be used to infer structure from a sample

text:

Consider the shape to the right.

title: What is a measurement?
text:
Analytical Measurements

Most analytical measurements look like (\(x\),\(y\))-data and can be thought of as \(n\)-dimensional; \(x\) is the property, and \(y\) is the measurement

Mass Spectrometry (abundance of ions with mass-to-charge ratio)
IR (percent transmittance at wave number)

We want to use analytical chemistry measurements to make decisions

Analytical measurements in forensic chemistry are subject to same issues as all measurements

uncertainty in the reference measurements
poor quality of the analyte
“unknowability” in the search space

And other specific issues

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Drug Identification

Discussion of drug prohibition in Canada started in the early 1900s as a response to opium

HIST-3790: Opium and the making of the modern world

Opium and Narcotics Drug Act passed in 1920; Controlled Drugs and Substances Act (last ammended July 2026)
Resources to learn more about the history of drug policy and other social considerations with drugs in Canada

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Drug Identification

Several major challenges (that can be addressed with new developments in science and technology)

Backlogs

Personnel turn around / training / lack of funding, emerging drugs

Novel Psychoactive Substances (Designer Drugs)

Making $3 million dollars of fentanyl using $3,600 and a web browser
Lack of reference data, isomers, may need new SOPs, reporting criteria, for each new drug

Sample complexity

Highly toxic drugs means that street samples actually have minor amounts of controlled material

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Drug Identification

Some analytical solutions currently being researched include

Fast GC-MS; GC coupled with Cold EI-MS
Ambient Ionization Mass Spectrometry
GC-VUV / GC-IR
Benchtop NMR

Better data sharing and collaboration between forensic labs and cognate research areas (e.g., public health, intelligence)
Article: Forensic seized drug analysis: Current challenges and emerging analytical techniques


VUV - vacuum ultra violet spectroscopy

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Chemical Weapons

The convention on the prohibition of the development, production, stockpiling, and use of chemical weapons and of their destruction (the CWC) was signed in 1993 and put into force in 1997
Chemical weapons includes:

Munitions, devices, equipment specifically designed for employing munitions
Toxic chemicals and their precursors

57 line items: 42 individual compounds and 15 families of compounds (e.g., VX)

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Chemical Weapons


Organization for the prohibition of chemical weapons (OPCW) was established by countries to enforce the CWC

verification studies
retrospective and incidence response type investigations

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Fire Investigations

Fires can be accidental or deliberate (arson). Potential motivations for deliberate fires include:

intent to cover up other crimes (theft, murder)
insurance fraud
civil disorder (e.g., vandalism)
malicious intent / terrorism

Fire investigations begin without certainty as to whether a crime has been committed

Step 1 is to determine the merit of the assertion that the event is suspicious

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Fire Investigations

Traditionally broken into two different stages:

scene investigation to determine cause, origin and development/spread of fire
lab analysis of samples (when arson is suspected)

Scene investigators need to know necessary conditions for fire to be initiated and maintained, how fires develop and spread (dynamics), different types of fuel, among other investigation skills
Lab Analysts need to have skills with analytical instrumentation and an understanding of the nature of flammable materials and their pyrolysis and combustion products to analyze fire residue/debris

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Fire Investigations

Some relevant material properties include:







Flammability (explosive) limits/ranges: outside of these limits, the fuel-vapor to air concentration will be too lean or too rich to ignite (e.g., the lower FL for 100 octane petrol is 1.4%, the upper FL is 7.6%)
Vapor density: density of the fuel vapor relative to the density of air (density less than 1 will spread out at the ceiling, density greater than 1 will spread out at the floor)
Flash point: lowest temperature at which a liquid fuel produces a flammable vapor
Flame point: the lowest temperature at which a liquid fuel produces enough flammable vapor that it can be ignited
Auto-ignition temperature (AIT): temperature at which a fuel will ignite without any additional source of ignition




Knowing a material’s properties only helpful if you know what the material is

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Fire Investigations

Significant research in fire investigation: (Interpol Review)
Fire scenes are hard: sample quality is poor (post fire extinguishing, a lot of components in a fuel, and weathering)

On-site chemical analysis
Models

Laboratory reconstructions (e.g., weathering studies)
Computer models

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Fire Investigations

The Fire Behaviour of Fabrics Containing Dried Emollient Residues

Proof-of-concept study
Objective: Investigate the flammability of fabrics containing dried emollient on fabrics
Results: Fabrics that have dried emollients are very flammable

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Fire Investigations

Artificial intelligence and thermodynamics help solving arson cases

Proof-of-concept study
Objective: demonstrate how combining machine learning, thermodynamic modeling and quantum mechanics can predict the composition of unweathererd gasoline samples starting from weathered ones
Results: Built and an NN model assuming an ideal case, where all composition change in gasoline is due exclusively to evaporation (and not adsorption, pyrolysis, degradation, extinguishing material)

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Death Investigation

Post-mortem examinations are carried out by pathologists to try and determine cause of death
Post-mortem examinations begin without certainty as to whether a crime has been committed 
Time since death is an important factor when trying to determine the cause of death

post-mortem interval (PMI) estimatition techniques are methods for approximating time since death

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Death Investigation

Several established techniques for PMI estimation:

Pathology (looking at post-mortem changes to the body)
Entomology (insect activity)

Newer techniques being researched:

DNA quantification (e.g., methylation)
Biomarker discovery

“OMICS” (metabolomics, lipidomics, and proteomics)
Looking at body (skin, hair, bones), environment (soil, water, air), microbes

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Death Investigation

The ‘ForensOMICS’ approach for postmortem interval estimation from human bone by integrating metabolomics, lipidomics, and proteomics

Proof-of-Concept study
Objective: To evaluate the utility of combining metabolomic, lipidomic, and proteomic analysis of human bone samples to estiamte PMI–“ForensOMICS”
Results: Showed that fingerprints of samples collected at different time points were best separated using metabolite information; infer that “ForensOMICS” can be used to estimate PMI

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Environmental Forensic Chemistry

A field that has developed over the past 70 years

A successor to drinking water quality studies

Involves scientific investigation to:

Decipher the source(s) and fate(s) of environmental contaminants
Identify culprit

Enforcement and protections of acts and regulations: Environment and Climate Change Canada Acts & Regulations

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Environmental Forensic Chemistry

The credibility of environmental forensic chemistry results is directly related to the quality of measurements and interpretations
Some well-known challenges in measurement quality include:

Sensitivity / Specificity
Changing targets (laws and regulations)
Sampling (environmental systems are complex)

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Environmental Forensic Chemistry

Case Study: Characterizing Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)
PFAS: group of thousands of synthetic chemicals that are used in consumer products and industrial processes

Non-stick cookware, cosmetics, cleaning products, food packaging
firefighting foam, lab equipment

Discovered in the 1930s; commonly used since the 1950s; started noticing environmental persistence and health effects in humans in the 1970s; subject of some environmental protection since 2000s

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Environmental Forensic Chemistry

Known health effects in animals:

liver damage, immune system malfunction, reproductive and developmental issues, tumors

Suspected health effects (correlations) in humans:

liver damage, increased serum cholesterol, decreased vaccination response, decreased birth weight, increased chance of thyroid disease, cardiovascular issues, cancer

Several governing bodies have created standards for allowable levels of specific PFAS in consumer products and the environment

title: Application areas in forensic chemistry
text:
Environmental Forensic Chemistry

Source attribution of Poly- and Perfluoralkyl Substances (PFASs) in surface waters from Rhode Island and New York Metropolitan Area
Objective: Identify sources of surface water PFAS contamination in a specified geography
Methods (summary):

sampled water at 28 sites in Rhode Island and 9 sites in NY/NJ
samples were spiked with known amount of PFAS
PFAS were then extracted and then analyzed using LC/MS-MS
Statistical and spatial analysis

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Basics of programming

Many modern scientific problems/tasks are too larger or too complex (or both) to solve without the aid of computers

some problems are hard to even visualize/imagine without computers

Programming is the act of providing computers with specific operational instructions; usually to assist (us) with performing a specific task or solving a specific problem
Can provide instructions via mouse and keyboard (i.e., use a software tool); but the majority of programming (coding) is done through written instructions called source code

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Basics of programming

the programming language used to write source code depends on:

the hardware/software of the computer (or instrument)

i.e., what can the computer process/understand

the task/problem being worked on
the skills/experience of the programmer

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Basics of programming

one major dichotomy to know:

Compiled Languages: source code gets compiled by an operating system specific compiler into an executable file (application) that can then be run directly by the operating system

language has a steeper learning curve, but the resulting applications run very efficiently 

Interpreted Languages: source code is executed by an interpreter (application) which being run on the operating system

language is more human-readable, but usually inefficient 


In this class we’ll be working with the R programming language

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Programming in R

To write R code, all you need is to know the language!
To run R code, all you need to have is:

A computer with any modern operating system (Windows, Max, Linux)
A text editor installed on the computer
The appropriate version of “R” (the interpreter) installed on the computer www.cran.r-project.org 

RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) application

allows you to view/edit code, run the code, visualize outputs in a console, and view all the variables currently loaded in the interpreting environment

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Errors

syntax are the set of rules/procedures for working with a language (grammarPlus)

compilers/interpreters are very sensitive to syntax–you need to follow the rules of your language for your code to run (syntax errors) 

compilers/interpreters are more literal than humans

you need to make sure your logic is precise for your code to output the correct answer (logic errors)

if your computer is not following the instructions you’ve provided, there is either a syntax error, a logic error, or a memory leak

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Some key R syntax


#                   # ignores text that follows until the next line (comment)
x <- 7              # create a variable x and assign it the value 7
y = 8               # create a variable y and assign it the value 8
z = x + y           # create a variable z and assign it the value of x + y
zebra = x^2         # create a variable zebra and assigned the value of x to the power 2





print(zebra)            # the function "print" displays the value of zebra maintaining its "shape"





ebra = zebra - z      # creates a variable ebra and assign it the value of zebra - z
cat(ebra)             # the function "cat" displays the value of variable ebra





cat(zebra - z)      # the function "cat" displays the value of variable zebra - z

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Some key R syntax


cat("This is a test")   # display the string "This is a test"
# cat(test)             # this code will fail because there is no variable named test in our environment





zebra_sentence = paste0("The value of zebra is ",zebra) # The paste0 function will glue things together without including any spaces
cat(zebra_sentence)





cat(paste0("The value of ebra is ",ebra) )

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Objects in R

Some key types of objects to be aware of:

variable: stores a single value, can be a number or character
array: stores multiple values, can contain numbers XOR characters (vectors + matrices)
data frames: multiple arrays, can be any data type but will force a “shape” on the data
lists: multiple variables, arrays, etc.. can be any data type AND any shape




 rm(list=ls())        # the ls() function finds all objects in the environment, the rm() function removes and lists that are provided to it
 
 x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) # creates an array x and assigns it the values 1 through 5 using the the "collect" function
 y = seq(1,5,1)       # creates an array y and assigns it the values 1 through 5 increments of 1 using the "sequence" function
 z = seq(1,5,0.1)     # creates an array z and assigns it the values 1 through 5 by increments of 0.1 using the "sequence"

text:
Objects in R


 xy = cbind(x,y)      # use the "cbind" function create a matrix xy with columns equal to x and y
 print(xy)

[3,] 3 3
[4,] 4 4

text:
Importing data in R

R is a general purpose programming language, but it is popular because of its rich repository of powerful statistics and data analysis functions

Reading and writing data
Regression modeling
Hypothesis testing
Machine learning




  rm(list=ls())                 # clear work space
  Spec1 = read.table("U1.txt")  # create an array Spec1 and assign it the values from the text file U1.txt using the read.table function
  # the first column is m/z values and second column are intensity values
  nPeaks = nrow(Spec1)          # create a variable nPeaks and assign it the value of the number of rows in the array Spec1 using the nrow function
  nPeaks                        # instead of using the print or cat function, in the console we can just type the variable name and its value will get printed on the screen

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Work with mass spectral data


plot(Spec1) # use the plot function to create a scatter plot of the x,y value in Spec1









Issues: atypical for plotting mass spectra (raw abundance scores, and scatter plot)

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Work with mass spectral data


mz = Spec1[,1]      # with an array, we can extract specific columns, rows and cell values
int = Spec1[,2]     
int = int/max(int)  # normalizes the intensity values to 1

plot(mz,
     int,
     type="h",
     xlab="mass-to-charge ratio",
     ylab="relative intensity") # use the plot function to create a scatter plot of the x,y value in Spec1


 Issues: a lot of low intensity peaks that could be artifacts

title: An introduction to programming with R
text:
Work with mass spectral data


noisePeaks = which(int<=0.01) # identify the values in the intensity array that have relative intensity less than 1%

if(length(noisePeaks)>0){   # checks to see if any noise peaks were identified, if yes runs code in the "chunck"
  mz = mz[-noisePeaks]
  int = int[-noisePeaks]
}

plot(mz,
     int,
     type="h",
     xlab="mass-to-charge ratio",
     ylab="relative intensity") # use the plot function to create a scatter plot of the x,y value in Spec1



Homework challenge: write some code to determine the mass-to-charge ratio of the base peak of this spectrum

text:
Working in the console versus writing a script

Why write and save scripts?

allows you to easily update and re-run your source code
allows you to share your source code with other people

Why work in the console?

to test some ideas out or compute something quickly

>90% of the time, you’ll want to write a script

title: Course Preliminaries+Introduction to Forensic Chemistry
text:
What is forensic chemistry?



Forensic chemistry is a phrase used to describe the application of chemistry to analyze evidence involved with suspected/potential criminal activity
The branch of chemistry predominantly associated with traditional forensic chemistry is analytical chemistry

title: Course Preliminaries+Introduction to Forensic Chemistry
text:
Forensic Chemist vs. Analytical Chemist

Exploratory vs. confirmatory
Emphasis on quality control measures (in lab and reporting)

more restrictive SOPs and maintenance schedules
more substantial peer review of reports

Testifying

Results must be able to stand up to adversarial questioning

Ethics and professionalism
Resourcefulness

title: Course Preliminaries+Introduction to Forensic Chemistry
text:
A forensic chemist’s traditional toolbox

Elemental Analysis

ICP-MS, SEM-EDS

Molecular Analysis

Colour/Spot Test, GC-FID, HPLC, Capillary Electrophoresis, GC-MS, LC-MS, ATR-FTIR, Raman, XRD




Choice of tool depends on several factors:

What are you analyzing? (solids vs liquids vs gas, mixtures vs pure compounds)
What do you need to know? (discriminating power, sensitvity)
Budget (purchase cost, maintenance cost, sample prep, cost-per-analysis)

ICP-MS: Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry

SEM-EDS: Scanning electron microscopy - energy dispersive x-ray spectroscopy
Colour/Spot tests: assays
HPLC: High performance liquid chromatography
GC-MS: Gas chromatography mass spectrometry
ATR-FTIR : Attenuated Total Reflection Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy
LC-MS: liquid chromatography mass spectrometry
Raman spectroscopy
XRD: x-ray diffraction crystallography

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Why develop new techniques?

improve sensitivity

extract more information from sample
extract information from less sample

improve specificity

extract more useful information from sample 

improve speed
improve portability
improve costs



speed could mean sample prep, acquisition and analysis
portability could mean taking things on the road, moving things between labs, etc.
costs could mean initial investment or operating costs or training costs

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Ambient ionization mass spectrometry
 HISTORY

Techniques were first reported in the literature in 2004

Desorpition electrospray ionization (DESI)
Direct Analysis in Real Time (DART) 

Developed as an alternative to standard mass spectrometry which required (1) ionization take place in a vacuum system, and (2) extensive sample preparation
Significantly faster method of generating mass spectra

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Ambient ionization mass spectrometry

Three main strategies for ionization at atmospheric pressure:

Ion-molecular reaction
Photochemical ionization
Charged droplets

Three main strategies for liberating analytes from sample without extensive sample preparation:

Liquid extractions
Thermal/Chemical Desorption (Plasma)
Spallation (Laser Ablation)

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Ambient ionization mass spectrometry

Over 30 unique ambient ionization mass spectrometry techniques described in the scientific literature (with over 30 citations each)















 LF: from Venter et al. (2014) RF: from Fieder et al. (2019)

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Ambient ionization mass spectrometry
LIMITATIONS

Desorbed materials can be a complex multi-compound mixture, especially in truly ambient applications

Competitive ionization / ion suppression
Sensitivity / LOD
Less control over operating parameters - more research to be done

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Ambient ionization mass spectrometry
AVAILABILITY

Many users build custom ambient ionization techniques and use with available (LC) mass spectrometry 
Many commercial options available:

Bruker (IonSense) DART-MS
Thermofisher VeriSpray
Waters RADIAN ASAP
Plasmion SICRIT

COSTS

Less sample preparation means less training, however the data analysis is more complicated

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Gas Chromatography

Gas chromatography (GC) is a popular form of chromatography

Vapor Phase Chromatography (VPC)
Gas Liquid Partition Chromatography

Liquid or gas sample is mixed with a non-reactive carrier gas and then passes through a column
Compounds separate according to chemical and physical properties

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Gas Chromatography



Can change parameters of GC system (e.g., carrier gas flow rate, oven temperature), which can change how compounds separate
Can change column length or lining material, which may change how compounds separate

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Gas Chromatography

CHALLENGE

Coelution is when two (or more) compounds in the analyte do not “clearly” separate
Can be a significant issue with complex mixtures with a lot of components at various concentrations

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
GC x GC

Two-dimensional gas chromatography (GC x GC) is a technique where two columns with different material linings are used to further increase separation

A modulator is used to concentrate eluent prior to being injected into second column

This concept can be extended to “higher dimensions”

Scales poorly due to cost (and reproducibility)

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
GC x GC

As of 2018, GC x GC has not met the Daubert criteria
The first accredited GC x GC method for analysis of persistent organic pollutants was developed by the Canadian Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
GC x GC

Not used in casework, but lots of research use across forensic disciplines

Human scent / taphonomy
Arson investigation
Drugs, CW, Explosives
Environment

Gruber et al. (2018)

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
GC Infrared Spectroscopy
 HISTORY

Technique first described in the literature in 1964 
Developed as an alternative to GC-MS which can better discriminate structural isomers 
Several iterations and modifications on the original GC-IR design over the last 50 years; most prominent system now is GC-FTIR

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
GC Infrared Spectroscopy
 MECHANISMS

GC is used to separate the sample components
IR Spectroscopy is used to characterize components based on absorption properties

Absorption properties tell us about presence/absence of “functional groups”; can be used to infer structure

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
GC Infrared Spectroscopy

Similar application areas as GC-MS

Environmental Analysis: detecting pollutants in air/water/soil
Forensic Science: crime scene chemicals, “chemical fingerprint”
Pharmaceutical Analysis: quality control, discovery
Food and Flavor Analysis: quality control, discovery

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
GC Infrared Spectroscopy
LIMITATIONS

Sensitivity (need a lot of sample to get a reasonable signal)
Sensitivity improves using FTIR

50 years of research have greatly improved sensitivity
Isotope analysis

Lack of generally accepted databases for searching/identification

text:

ThermoFisher

COSTS

GC sample preparation, more sample needed given lower sensitivity

Miniaturization and Portable Techniques



Spectrometers have decreased in size over the past 20 years

optical spectrometers
mass spectrometers

Trending towards smaller and more rugged instrumentation, enabling portable analysis

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text: Miniaturization and Portable Techniques

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Miniaturization and Portable Techniques

Ion Mobility Spectroscopy (IMS)

Illicit drugs; explosives
Pros: low LOD; simple to operate; no sample preparation
Cons: presumptive ID (high FPR); destructive; potential to overload detector; long start-up time 

Fourier Transform Inferred Spectroscopy (FT-IR)

Breath alcohol; illicit drugs; counterfeit drugs; explosives
Pros: non-destructive; highly selective; simple to operate; no consumables
Cons: high LOD; mixtures

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Miniaturization and Portable Techniques

Raman Spectroscopy 

Illicit drugs; explosives; counterfeit drugs
Pros: non-destructive, highly selective; no contact required; simple to use
Cons: high LOD; mixtures; fluorescence (interference) 

Gas Chromatography Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS)

Illicit drugs; counterfeit drugs; explosives; ignitable liquids
Pros: high selectivity; low LOD; mixtures; standards/libraries
Cons: destructive; high cost; isomers

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Miniaturization and Portable Techniques

Mass Spectrometry (MS)

Illicit drugs; explosives
Pros: high selectivity; low LOD
Cons: destructive; high cost; mixtures; isomers

High Pressure Mass Spectrometry (HP-MS)

Illicit drugs; explosives
Pros: low LOD; size
Cons: presumptive ID (high FPR); incomparable to traditional mass spectral data

title: Emerging analytical techniques in forensic chemistry
text:
Miniaturization and Portable Techniques

As of 2021, most portable techniques have not been generally adopted in crime investigation

Perceived costs and complexity
Lack of training / hesitancy to learn new techniques / too big a change

Crocombe et al. (eds) Portable Spectroscopy and Spectrometry Volumes 1 and 2, 2021.
